title: Top 15: Vanke — We Read Vanke's Executive Roster. Vanke, You're Getting Old
body:
## Can This Elephant of Chinese Real Estate Still Dance?

Regular article

It was probably the personnel change that mattered most to Vanke in the past year. On March 9, Mao Daqing, senior vice president of Vanke Group and general manager of Vanke Beijing, announced that he was leaving to start his own business.

In his five years at Vanke, Mao served in turn as vice president, executive vice president and senior vice president of the group; as general manager and then chairman of the Beijing company; and as chief executive of the Beijing region.

When Mao joined Vanke in 2009, Vanke Beijing's sales stood at 4.3 billion yuan. In 2014 they topped 20 billion RMB, up 365.1% from 2009 and well ahead of the 239.2% growth of Vanke Group as a whole. Vanke itself had by then become a company with more than 200 billion yuan in sales.

"He turned Vanke Beijing around and made Vanke the leader of the Beijing market. His departure is clearly a loss for Vanke," Vanke president Yu Liang told reporters earlier.

Mao's successor, Liu Xiao, joined Vanke in the same year as Mao. Counting his new post, he has held seven titles in five years at the company.

Liu is 11 years younger than Mao. At 36, he is the youngest member of Vanke Group's management.

What has put Vanke in the spotlight lately is Harbor City in Tianjin. At about 11:30 p.m. on August 12, a stack of hazardous chemicals stored by Ruihai Logistics at the Tianjin port in the Binhai New Area exploded. So far 114 people have died and 65 are still missing. The nearest housing to the blast was Vanke Harbor City, where nearly every window on the side facing the explosion was shattered. Vanke Jinyu Lanwan, 1,000 meters away, was also badly damaged by the shock wave.

This may be the biggest thing to happen to Vanke this year, but it has nothing to do with the company's business, so it shows up in the general news pages rather than the business pages. That happens now and then. And because it is unrelated to the business, it has done nothing to the company's results.

In fact, according to Vanke's newly released interim report for 2015, first-half revenue and profit rose 22.7% and 27.2% year on year. In 2014 its sales also passed 200 billion yuan.

What people do remember is that Vanke has been doing some "Internet Plus" things.

At the start of 2014, Yu Liang took his management team to internet companies such as Xiaomi, Alibaba and Tencent to learn from them. In August, Vanke Group launched Wanxianghui, a WeChat-based marketing tool that anyone could join. After that, Vanke teamed up with Taobao to sell homes...

"The whole culture at Vanke strongly encourages young people to innovate. I think the hunger for innovation has gone beyond encouragement. It's anxiety," said Xia Tian, 28, who joined Vanke last May and works in marketing management for one of its regions. "Whether the outside world calls it crossing into other industries or embracing the internet, the anxiety ends up taking a concrete form: they want employees to innovate and to start more new businesses. Facing the internet, and facing the state of the whole industry, Vanke hopes to make some kind of breakthrough," she told QDaily.

According to Xia, Vanke has an internal trial-and-error committee that encourages young people to experiment boldly, and nobody is held responsible if something goes wrong. If an idea works, it can quickly spread from one city company to all the others. After Vanke Hangzhou partnered with Taobao, for example, Vanke Suzhou soon partnered with Dianping.

The "learning center" Vanke Hangzhou set up began as a community education program offering classes for children. This year it became the Vanke Hangzhou Education Group, run by someone born in the 1990s who has been with the company for two years.

Every Vanke project now has its own WeChat group. In her year or so at Vanke, Xia says, what her colleagues post about most is not what other developers are doing but what Xiaomi has done, or what Uber is up to now. "Ma Jiajia coming to give a talk at Vanke was just a louder signal to the outside world. Sessions like that happen all the time inside Vanke."

"In the past two years, Vanke's idea of talent has shifted toward people with a feel for asset-light models and the internet. It wants more people from outside real estate, from hotel management or the internet, for example, people who know how to use big-data analysis to target services and facilities at its residents," said Cao Xin, global partner and chief commercial officer for Greater China at the human resources consultancy Aon Hewitt. She told QDaily that her firm has advised Vanke on human resources since 2001.

All of this is probably part of Vanke's effort to remake itself as a "city services provider": regular contact with internet companies, study trips to Alibaba's headquarters, visits to Tencent and others, a partnership with Baidu to apply big data to community retail, a partnership with Taobao to sell homes...

Vanke really is trying to understand young people, but it looks rather like a middle-aged man trying to understand them: clumsy and a little lost.

After Mao left, Zhou Tong, general manager of the Shenzhen company; Sun Jia, general manager of the Shanghai company; Que Dongwu, general manager of Vanke's Hong Kong management department; and Wang Yun, general manager of the Vanke Architecture Research Center, became group vice presidents at the same time as Liu Xiao. Three of them were born in 1975 or later: Sun Jia is 37, Wang Yun is exactly 40, and Liu Xiao, at 36, is the youngest in Vanke's entire management.

From information on Vanke's website, QDaily calculated that the company's 20 senior executives now average about 48 years old, and the only ones born in 1975 or later are these three new appointees.

![Chart of the ages of Vanke's senior executives](/uploads/image/201508/0133b76f76cd.jpg)

This has to do with Vanke's history and with how it has produced its managers. At first, Vanke trained managers mainly on the job. After 1993, it trained them mainly in the classroom; Yu Liang, Guo Jun and Ding Changfeng came up this way.

Vanke listed on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange in 1991. Two years later, Wang Shi made mass-market housing the company's core business and cut the 17 other fields it had entered, a move outsiders see as the start of Vanke's "specialization." From 1993 to 2000, Vanke's revenue grew from 1.084 billion yuan to 3.873 billion yuan, an average of 36.8% a year.

In those days Wang Shi trained most people himself, and most of them were fresh college graduates. *Vanke Weekly*, which Wang founded in 1992, became an important training ground. Every one of its editors-in-chief was groomed by Wang and later given major responsibilities.

The first editor-in-chief, Guo Jun, went on to become general manager of Vanke Tianjin and vice general manager of Vanke Group. The second, Lin Shaozhou, became deputy general manager of Vanke Shanghai and then general manager of Vanke Beijing. The third, Ding Changfeng, became general manager of Vanke Shanghai, vice general manager of Vanke Group and general manager of the northern region, among other posts. The fourth, Quan Zhong, served as deputy general manager of Vanke Chengdu...

The editor of *Vanke Weekly* held a special place at Vanke. Reportedly, the job came with almost no requirements of seniority, experience or track record, yet its holder could attend every top-level decision-making meeting and speak freely. These new graduates did bring bold ideas, and they even argued with Wang Shi, who encouraged it and praised them for it. When Guo Jun, the first editor, left the job to run Vanke Tianjin, he was only 26.

![Chart of Vanke Weekly's editors-in-chief and their later posts](/uploads/image/201508/f33489ef1e92.jpg)

In 2001, Yu Liang took over as Vanke's president from Wang Shi. He, too, was just 36.

From the 1990s on, Vanke's talent was trained personally by Wang Shi, and its managers averaged only about 35 years old. Ding Changfeng, now a senior vice president, was only 30 when he became general manager of Vanke Shanghai (in 2000), and Yu Liang was only 29 when he joined Vanke's board (in 1994).

That was also a period of fast expansion for Vanke.

![Chart of Vanke's management ages and expansion in its early years](/uploads/image/201508/2a91e0b05812.jpg)

In the round of appointments that followed Mao Daqing's departure in March, Yu Liang raised the question of age for the first time.

In earlier personnel changes, Vanke seldom drew public attention to its executives' ages. With these appointments, Yu Liang also announced a new staffing rule: "Use both old and new, with the new in the lead." Because "their future decides Vanke's future, so we have to make this bet."

Vanke seems to have realized that it is getting old.

"In how he uses people and manages talent, what we saw in Yu Liang early on was mostly continuity," Cao Xin told QDaily. Vanke came to her firm in 2001, just as Wang Shi was handing the reins to Yu Liang. She clearly remembers that Wang Shi signed the early parts of the project contract, while Yu Liang signed the final plan.

After Yu Liang took over, Vanke began a new round of expansion. Compared with the headlong, unplanned growth of the 1990s, Vanke now aimed for pacing and planning. In 2000 it drew up a group plan covering 2000 to 2004, the first "five-year plan" in its history.

In his memoir *My 20 Years with Vanke*, Wang Shi wrote: "The company is entering a growth phase. Strengthening the professional manager class and making effective use of a well-trained corps of professional managers will directly help an increasingly specialized enterprise become more competitive, adapt to the competitive environment and keep growing."

Meanwhile, the Asian financial crisis that began in the second half of 1997 shook the market, and Chinese companies began to face the tide of the "knowledge economy" and "global market integration." Vanke needed more capable professional managers, and at the same time those managers had begun to move freely between employers.

Vanke made 1998 its year of the professional manager in human resources. In 2000, it launched a poaching campaign code-named "Pirate," aimed at China Overseas Land & Investment, which had lost heavily in the 1997 Asian financial crisis. China Overseas had a rigorous system for developing talent. By 2004, 40% of the managers running Vanke's front-line companies were core staff from China Overseas, which filled Vanke's shortage of front-line general managers as it expanded.

Alongside this expansion, Vanke also worked on its brand and hired an internationally known 4A advertising agency.

In 2007, Vanke's sales passed 50 billion RMB for the first time, up 146.6% year on year, and the company began preparing to become a business with 100 billion yuan in sales. That year it launched a recruiting plan code-named "Operation 007," more often called the "social elite campaign" in public. It marked an important change in Vanke's approach to human resources: bringing in outsiders rather than relying only on internal promotion.

Its targets were people who had actually run, or worked at, companies with 100 billion yuan in sales. Mao Daqing was the last recruit of "Operation 007." Yu Liang said it took two years and more than 20 dinners to win him over, and the deal was sealed only when Chairman Wang Shi stepped in himself. Before that, Mao had worked at Singapore Land for 15 years.

Liu Xiao was another recruit of the plan. Before joining Vanke he worked at McKinsey, and he holds an MBA from Harvard Business School. Before taking over Vanke Beijing, Liu was general manager of Vanke Hangzhou, where in two and a half years he grew sales from 4 billion yuan to the current 15 billion yuan. Vanke's "three goods" idea, "good homes, good service, good communities," also originated with him.

![Chart of Vanke executives recruited from outside](/uploads/image/201508/2612972838c8.jpg)

In 2001, Aon Hewitt in China worked mostly for multinationals; Vanke was only the second Chinese company to hire it for human resources consulting. "Vanke also put forward a very forward-looking concept at the time, a numerical talent model, meaning a definition of what kind of people Vanke actually needs," Cao Xin said. In Vanke's talent model, the first quality every employee must have is to "be good": to focus on results and do one's own job conscientiously. For senior executives, it is to "be better": to think ahead and innovate.

As Vanke moved through different stages, its talent needs changed too. "As it faced more challenges, Yu Liang kept adjusting how he managed talent, but the basic principles never changed."

But Vanke now faces a much harsher market. Some say that with Mao Daqing's departure, the last five years of the golden age of Vanke, and of Chinese real estate as a whole, have ended as well. Mao himself thinks it will be hard to top the peak of 20 billion yuan in sales, and profits are getting thinner and thinner.

It is not just Vanke. The word the whole property industry used most last year was "transformation." Yu Liang sees promoting young people as an unavoidable choice in the transformation. "There are risks, but Vanke is willing to bet its risks and its future on them." Yet it looks more like a move made because there was no other choice.

Before Mao Daqing, Vanke had already lost several waves of executives. The first to go was vice president Chen Dongfeng (in October 2010). Then, in January 2011, vice president Xiao Nan and executive vice president Xu Hongge left together. Xu was one of Vanke's longest-serving people, second in rank only to Wang Shi and Yu Liang, and widely tipped as Vanke's "third-generation" leader. By one count, nine veterans of the "Wang Shi era," all at vice president level, have left Vanke since Yu Liang took charge: Chen Dongfeng, Mao Daqing, Xu Hongge and Xiao Nan, plus Xu Guohong, Liu Aiming, Du Jing, Yuan Boyin and Xiao Li.

![Chart of senior executives who have left Vanke](/uploads/image/201508/80d754d104e1.jpg)

Many of the departed executives have gone into internet ventures. Chen Dongfeng joined Yonyou Software, Xiao Li joined Fangduoduo, an online real estate services platform, and Mao Daqing has said he will build a Chinese version of WeWork, offering space to young entrepreneurs.

That may also have put Yu Liang on alert. At a time when the internet is hitting, reshaping and even upending every industry, how can Vanke turn gracefully into the internet era? He hopes young people will bring unconventional ideas with their way of thinking.

The experiments go on. Last year Vanke introduced a partnership system to keep talent. In April this year, Yu Liang signed the *Vanke Group Measures for Managing Internal Entrepreneurship*, which says: "Employees are encouraged to start businesses within the Vanke ecosystem, help Vanke build and enrich that ecosystem, and create value for customers." Some have read this document, which encourages employees to quit and start businesses, as layoffs in disguise.

On arriving in Beijing, Liu Xiao set up a "performance improvement team" and a "business strategy implementation team," which together cover all of Vanke Beijing's day-to-day management, operations and strategy. Vanke Beijing has also introduced V-LINK, a community system meant to drive product innovation.

"We are in the middle of a transformation. What do we do in the next ten years? We are confused. We discussed it for eight months and still haven't figured it out," Wang Shi said at a summit in 2014, voicing the same anxiety. Facing a market in flux, Vanke may really have grown old. Can this elephant of the property world dance?

(Liu Ximing also contributed to this article.) (Xia Tian is a pseudonym, used at the interviewee's request.)

Graphics: Lin Yuyao

## About Top 15

In every era, a few companies gather the most capital and the best people and shape how society develops. QDaily believes that the companies that shape the way we live are at the heart of today's business world.

So we have chosen the 15 most important lifestyle companies in the world and in China: [Apple](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/8963.html), [Google](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/7936.html), [Baidu](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/11837.html), [Alibaba](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/9234.html), [Tencent](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/9876.html), [Amazon](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/9501.html), [Disney](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/10031.html), [McDonald's](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/9029.html), [Starbucks](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/9988.html), [Nike](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/13114.html), [Xiaomi](http://www.qdaily.com/display/articles/9564.html), [IKEA](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/9550.html), [Uniqlo](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/10978.html), [Wanda](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/11480.html) and Vanke. The list will change as the companies' businesses, markets and trends change. We will follow them, and their competitors and partners too.
